about: The epistola of the formulary “Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed — Mass I” in the 1962 Roman Missal.

seg.tr: Brethren: Behold, I tell you a mystery: All of us will indeed rise again, but not all of us will be changed. In an instant, in the blink of an eye, at the final trumpet — for the trumpet will ring out, and the dead will rise again incorrupt, and we will be changed, since this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. And when this mortal has put on immortality, the saying that is written will then be fulfilled: Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? And the sting of death is sin, while sin’s strength is the law. But to God be thanks, who gave us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

a.g: we will not all be changed

ex.w011: “Not all” limits who will be changed. It does not mean that no one will be changed.
ex.w027: In this resurrection context, the adjective describes the condition of the dead as they rise, free from bodily decay.
ex.w033: The phrase points to this body, which is subject to decay. The gloss includes “body”, understood from the context, and uses the English construction “for … to” to express necessity.
ex.w046: The clothing with immortality is complete before the saying comes to pass. English naturally uses “has put on” after “when” for this future-completed action.
ex.w077: The second statement leaves “is” unexpressed in Latin, continuing the parallel with the preceding sentence. It identifies the law as the power of sin.
